name: Islamic feminism
summary: Islamic feminism seeks equality and justice for women and men within an Islamic framework. It holds that patriarchal readings of the Qur'an and classical jurisprudence, not Islam itself, produced discriminatory family laws and practices, and it calls for reinterpretation (ijtihad), women's equal voice in defining Islam, and legal reform backed by constitutions and human-rights standards.
scope: The mainstream faith-based reformist strand as articulated by Amina Wadud, Asma Barlas, Margot Badran and the Musawah movement and Sisters in Islam (Malaysia), based on the Musawah Framework for Action. It excludes secular Muslim feminists who reject the label and conservative Islamist women's movements. The movement is mostly about gender, family law and religious authority, so many economic and foreign-policy statements are inferred or neutral.

keyFigures.name: Amina Wadud
keyFigures.role: Scholar whose contextual reading of Qur'an 4:34 stresses mutual responsibility between men and women.

keyFigures.name: Asma Barlas
keyFigures.role: Author of Believing Women in Islam, arguing the Qur'an encourages full equality of women and men.

keyFigures.name: Zainah Anwar
keyFigures.role: Leading figure of Sisters in Islam and member of the Musawah planning committee.

sources.usedFor: Positions on hudud, apostasy, polygamy, dress, domestic violence, and religious authority.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Not a central issue for the movement; its commitment to dignity and equal access to resources suggests support for public provision, but this is inferred.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Monetary institutions are outside the movement's concerns and adherents hold no shared view.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: The movement has no position on corporatist wage-setting; adherents span the economic spectrum.

one-party-rule.rationale: Musawah's call for equal citizenship and participation of all in shaping laws is incompatible with a single ideological party monopoly.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Islamic feminists live under monarchies and republics alike and the movement takes no stand on the form of the head of state.

democracy-best.rationale: Sisters in Islam and Musawah ground their claims in constitutional rights and citizen participation, though the exact formulation 'even when voters choose badly' is untested.

direct-votes.rationale: Direct legislation is not discussed; adherents focus on who shapes religious law rather than referendum mechanics.

workers-councils.rationale: The movement works through constitutions, courts and parliaments for family-law reform, not councils; inferred.

right-to-secede.rationale: Secession is not addressed by the movement and adherents are divided by national context.

natural-rulers.rationale: Islamic feminists argue that no group is naturally superior; Barlas says the Qur'an rejects the idea that men are born to rule women.

political-violence-never.rationale: Movement activism is nonviolent and campaigns against terror groups, but no doctrine of absolute pacifism is stated; inferred.

war-builds-character.rationale: Nothing in the movement's texts glorifies war, and its emphasis on compassion and mutual respect points against it; inferred.

separate-church-state.rationale: Most Islamic feminists reject strict separation, arguing for engaging Islam as a source of values; secular Muslim feminists who disagree reject the Islamic feminist label itself.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Musawah says laws must reflect Islamic values of justice and equality yet insists family laws are human-made fiqh, not divine; this is not a call for laws derived directly from scripture, though it is not rejected outright.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Adherents look to the state, constitution and courts to guarantee equality, so privatizing justice is unlikely to be favored; inferred.

military-superiority.rationale: Foreign policy and military power are outside the movement's agenda.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Musawah rests on universal equality and non-discrimination and a global Muslim community of many nations, which contradicts ethnic nationhood.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The movement is not built on a theory of class conflict; some adherents are leftist, others liberal or conservative.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Musawah demands equal rights and substantive equality between women and men but takes no stance on equal economic outcomes generally.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Adherents criticize colonial influence on family laws (Leila Ahmed, Musawah) but reparations are not a stated demand.

civilizational-union.rationale: The movement stresses citizenship in modern nations and global human rights; political union of Muslim states is not part of it; inferred.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Its ethic of mutual responsibility, compassion and justice runs against celebrating self-interest; inferred.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Musawah makes equal rights the core demand and criticizes duties like wifely obedience being used to deny rights to women.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: The environment is not a theme of the movement; Islamic ethics might support intrinsic value but no source states it.

limit-population.rationale: Adherents stress women's autonomy over their lives and oppose coercion, so coercive limits are disfavored; no stated position.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The movement does not share a critique of industrial civilization and generally embraces modern education and rights; inferred.

accelerate-technology.rationale: No position; technology is not a concern of the movement.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Adherents emphasize human participation and accountability in law-making; inferred.

restore-past-order.rationale: Musawah and Barlas hold that classical patriarchal orders were products of their era and must change; restoring a lost order is the opposite of reform.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The movement argues from principle, justice and maslahah (public interest) together; it takes no stand on pragmatism versus ideology.

direct-action.rationale: Advocacy is mainly through legal reform, petitions to courts and religious argument, though protest is used (for example Sisters in Islam campaigns); inferred.

means-match-ends.rationale: No documented position on this principle.

return-to-foraging.rationale: The movement is committed to education, modern law and human rights, so a return to foraging is entirely foreign to it.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Not addressed; adherents challenge gendered roles but not the division of labor itself.

distribute-by-need.rationale: No stated position; Musawah calls for equal property rights and financial security of family members but not needs-based distribution.

production-for-use.rationale: The movement does not address how production should be organized.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Not part of the movement's analysis, which centres on patriarchy rather than capitalist exploitation.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Rule by one class over others contradicts the movement's equal-citizenship principle.

collective-farming.rationale: Farm organization is not addressed by the movement's thinkers.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Not part of the movement's analysis.

taxation-theft.rationale: Adherents see the state as the guarantor of rights and not as an illegitimate coercer; inferred.

harm-principle.rationale: Many adherents defend personal choice, as in opposing forced veiling, while still working within Islamic moral frameworks; no common position.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Musawah blends individual rights with family and community, and Islamic framings of duty and community stay important to adherents.

conscription.rationale: Military service is not discussed; adherents differ by country and women's service is not a stated demand.

exit-over-voice.rationale: The movement's whole strategy is voice, claiming a right to define Islam and shape laws from within communities.

state-as-business.rationale: Citizens are rights-holders in the movement's framework, not customers; inferred.

positive-liberty.rationale: Musawah ties equality to access to economic resources and dignified choices, which implies material means for freedom; inferred.

media-academia-power.rationale: Claims about media and academic power are not part of Islamic feminist argument.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Equal worth and dignity of all human beings is a foundational principle of Musawah; racial hierarchy contradicts it.

organic-representation.rationale: Adherents seek full individual citizenship and participation, not representation via families and corporate bodies; inferred.

total-state.rationale: Equal citizenship, constitutional guarantees and women's autonomy conflict with a state directing all of life.

national-rebirth.rationale: The movement seeks gradual reform through reinterpretation, not national rebirth from decadence; inferred.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Nothing in the movement supports expansion; its values are justice and mutual respect.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Equal citizenship and constitutional rights rule out personal-oath authority.

bound-labor.rationale: Musawah explicitly compares family-law reform to the abolition of slavery and defends equal rights to dignity and property.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Islamic feminists argue that religious knowledge and jurisprudence have reflected the power of male jurists and that readings depend on who reads (Barlas, Musawah), though they still believe in a true message.

universal-morality.rationale: Musawah appeals to universal values of equality and dignity found in both Islam and human rights; its grounding is revelation as well as reason.

single-common-good.rationale: Musawah argues from maslahah and a diversity of opinion (ikhtilaf) rather than a single worked-out good; inferred.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Not a movement issue; adherents hold varied views by national context.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language revival is unrelated to the movement's concerns and adherents have no shared view.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Not addressed; some adherents might favor it but the movement has no position.

school-vouchers.rationale: School funding mechanisms are not addressed, though Musawah values equal access to education.

economic-freedom.rationale: No stated position on the relationship between economic and political freedom.

rule-by-example.rationale: Musawah seeks codified equal legal rights, not rule by rulers' moral example; inferred.

national-self-determination.rationale: Not addressed directly; adherents work within existing nation states.

force-without-un.rationale: Use of force abroad is not addressed in Musawah's texts or in Barlas's work.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Islamic feminists work within faith and treat revelation as a source of justice, not reason alone, though they use reasoned reinterpretation; secular Muslim feminists reject the label.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Welfare eligibility for migrants is not discussed in the sources.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Musawah's emphasis on dignity and care responsibilities makes work conditions for support unlikely to be favored; inferred.

class-collaboration.rationale: The movement analyzes gender relations, not employer-worker relations, so it takes no side.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Movement members argue from within the Islamic tradition and engage classical sources critically, not by discarding heritage.

dominated-front.rationale: Adherents are divided; many resist being cast as Western proxies while others are critical of Western powers.

workers-nation.rationale: Working-class internationalism versus nationalism is not a theme of Islamic feminism.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Musawah and Wadud reject law that assigns distinct male and female roles, calling for equal decision-making and equal rights.

ban-interest.rationale: Islamic finance is not a feminist issue; adherents hold varied views.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Equality and non-discrimination are foundational; racial segregation is rejected.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Not part of the movement's analysis.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Fossil fuel policy is outside the movement's sources and has no shared adherent view.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Adherents often defend the right of Muslims to practice faith and dress in minority settings; inferred.

elite-replacement.rationale: This conspiracy view conflicts with the movement's universal-equality principles and its defence of Muslim minorities.

national-mission.rationale: Not part of the movement's views; its framing is universal not national.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Adherents criticize male religious and political establishments but have no general anti-elite doctrine.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Equal worth and dignity of all, plus women's autonomy, rule out eugenic restrictions.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Musawah emphasises justice and legal accountability, and SIS has called for state accountability; inferred.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Adherents rely on state laws and courts to secure women's rights across many areas of life; inferred.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Equal worth and non-discrimination are core; Musawah promotes free choice of spouse.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Debates over socialist strategy do not touch Islamic feminist thought.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Not addressed; adherents hold varied views.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Adherents are split: some in Muslim-minority democracies reject personal law and use civil law, while others seek reformed Muslim family law (Wikipedia).

restrict-conversion.rationale: Sisters in Islam opposes penalties for apostasy and defends religious freedom, which implies opposing legal restriction of conversion.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Not a movement issue and Islamic food practice does not support a ban; inferred.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Adherents are divided between secular and faith-integrated schooling; the movement has no stated view.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A doctrine of socialist state strength is not part of the movement; its sources do not address it.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Musawah invokes constitutional guarantees and the right and duty of all to take part in shaping laws, consistent with legitimacy by consent.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist trade aims are not discussed by adherents.

population-transfer.rationale: Movement values of equal citizenship and dignity condemn forced removals of minorities.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: No stated position on strict non-aggression.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Its ethic of mutual respect and compassion points away from struggle as progress engine; inferred.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Adherents oppose fundamentalist groups but also defend freedoms against state moral policing; no common stance.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: The movement's complaint is male domination in marriage and law, with classical marriage described as domination by the husband, which fits the non-domination idea.

separated-powers.rationale: SIS has relied on constitutional courts and checks on religious authorities, including the 2014 fatwa challenge; inferred.

vanguard-party.rationale: Musawah calls for broad participation and everyone's equal right to interpret, not a vanguard.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Not a stated priority of the movement, though Islamic ethics values compassion.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Housing tenure policy is not in the movement's sources, though Musawah wants equal property rights for women.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Industrial relations law is not covered by Islamic feminist writers, who list labor rights only among areas touched by gender inequality.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Musawah locates injustice in unjust laws and institutions rather than population; inferred.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Musawah embraces diversity of opinion and non-discrimination, and adherents defend plural societies.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Not discussed; the movement seeks full political participation and leadership, not lotteries; inferred.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Musawah stresses constitutional guarantees and rights, and SIS challenges abuses of religious authority and law.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Price controls on food are not discussed in the movement's sources.

party-controls-media.rationale: Sisters in Islam has opposed state moral policing and fatwas against it, and free expression underpins its work.

party-commands-army.rationale: Not addressed directly; constitutional accountability is stressed so the idea is disfavoured; inferred.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Musawah campaigns on women's equal nationality rights, but the length of residence before naturalization is not addressed.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Pay for legislators is not addressed in any of the sources used.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Internal party discipline is not discussed; the movement is organized as networks and NGOs, not parties.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Not addressed; adherents rely on international instruments like CEDAW but have no stand on supranational unions.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The relation of head of state to the armed forces is not a topic in the sources.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Not applicable to Islam, which lacks bishops, though the movement opposes male monopoly over religious authority.

clerical-rule.rationale: Zainah Anwar says all women have an equal right to define Islam and must resist male domination of interpretation; Musawah says all Muslims have equal right to read the texts, rejecting rule by scholars.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Revolutionary defeatism is a Marxist-Leninist idea that the movement does not engage.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: SIS has opposed state moral policing and Musawah insists on women's dignified choices.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Not addressed; accountable constitutional government is favored; inferred.

recall-officials.rationale: Recall elections are not discussed, though equal political participation is endorsed.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Alliance policy is not addressed in Musawah or Barlas.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Abolishing renting is not part of the movement; only equal property ownership for women is stated.

people-in-arms.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the movement's reliance on lawful institutions.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Moral comparisons of rural and urban life do not appear in the sources.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: National reunification claims are not covered by the movement, which is organized across many countries.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The movement is led by academics and activists and values scholarship; inferred.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Adherents split: many defend the legitimacy of Muslim cultures but also criticize patriarchal customs that Musawah says are not defensible.

death-penalty.rationale: Adherents have no common position; SIS opposed hudud punishments and apostasy death penalties but broader capital punishment is not addressed.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: SIS and Muslim women's groups work on education about equality and reproductive health, and Musawah demands equality in education, but specific curricula are inferred.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Not addressed; adherents who use historically contextual reading accept modern science; inferred.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Musawah specifically campaigns for equal nationality rights for women to pass citizenship to children; a descent-only rule is not endorsed though not rejected by the movement outright.

minority-language-support.rationale: Language policy is not addressed by Islamic feminist writers.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Adherents split between defending religious freedom of Muslim minorities and opposing exemptions that harm women, as in the minority personal-law debate.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Adherents split between defending individual choice and working within Islamic norms.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Third-world debt is not discussed in the sources used, so no shared stance exists.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Adherents criticize colonial-era laws but do not tie independence to property-system change.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Not addressed, though broad participation in lawmaking fits the movement's principles.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Musawah insists on rights and equal participation without conditions.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Global aid duties are not addressed; Musawah's texts focus on family law in Muslim societies.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Nuclear deterrence is outside the movement's agenda.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Method of choosing the head of state is not discussed in the sources.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Central bank design is unrelated to the movement's concerns.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial bargains in peace talks are not addressed by the movement.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Musawah demands equal property rights for women but is silent on the general justification of property.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: The Soviet debate belongs to Marxist history and does not appear in Islamic feminist sources.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental risk regulation is not discussed in the sources.

collective-defense.rationale: Mutual-defense treaties are not addressed by the movement.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: International law on annexation is not discussed in the movement's sources.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Adherents want religious authorities accountable to constitutions, as in the SIS fatwa case, but do not seek to curb religion generally; mixed, inferred.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The role of a ceremonial head of state is not a movement concern.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Secession and force are not addressed in the sources used.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Special-autonomy arrangements are outside the movement's concerns.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Equal worth of all and the claim that all have equal rights to interpret religion rule out a sacred ruler.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Tax structure is not addressed by Islamic feminist writers.

character-from-environment.rationale: Islamic feminists argue gender differences are shaped by interpretation and social context, which implies upbringing matters; inferred.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Musawah invokes constitutional guarantees and equality before the law.

space-expansion.rationale: Space policy is irrelevant to the movement and not mentioned in the sources.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Classical mixed-regime theory is not part of Islamic feminist writing.

leader-cult.rationale: Equality and dismantling of male religious authority make leader worship alien to the movement.

equal-parenting.rationale: Musawah calls for equal rights and responsibilities of parents in matters relating to their children.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: This is an internal Marxist-Leninist question that the movement does not engage.

land-redistribution.rationale: Agrarian reform is not in the movement's sources, though Musawah wants equal property and inheritance for women.

refugee-return.rationale: Right of return is not addressed in the sources, and adherents' views vary with national context.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Not addressed; the movement's civic citizenship stress points against it; inferred.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Sisters in Islam opposed Kelantan's apostasy death-penalty bill and punishments for women who left the faith.

women-must-cover.rationale: Mainstream Islamic feminism supports voluntary veiling only; Barlas holds the Qur'an requires modesty but not veiling and My Stealthy Freedom opposes forced hijab; SIS reads the dress guidance as modesty and not a code.

common-currency.rationale: Currency union is outside the movement's agenda.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Pan-ethnic political unity is not part of the movement, which is organized around equality, not kin union.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Minority cultural self-government is not discussed in the sources.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The movement campaigns for equal rights in the countries where Muslims live, using constitutions; inferred for minorities.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Adherents argue religious interpretation was shaped by social conditions of classical jurists, but do not hold a materialist theory of history.

ban-cartels.rationale: Competition policy does not feature in the movement's sources.

no-bailouts.rationale: Bailout policy is not discussed by Islamic feminist authors.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Sisters in Islam and Musawah rely on constitutional guarantees and courts, including the Indian Supreme Court petition, to protect women against majority and religious-authority pressure.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Musawah demands equal rights to political participation and leadership; Islamic feminists seek women in clergy, administration and the judiciary, though quotas themselves are not stated.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Autarkic trade blocs are not part of the movement's thought.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Not addressed, though labour rights are named among areas of women's inequality.

moral-incentives.rationale: Debates on work motivation under socialism are absent from the sources.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The movement works through reinterpretation and law reform and campaigns against terrorist groups.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Equality and the denunciation of arbitrary privilege suggest support for abolishing hereditary titles; inferred.

history-own-civilization.rationale: The movement does not address how school history should be centered.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Leila Ahmed criticizes Qasim Amin's colonialist framing, and Islamic feminists reject colonial paternalism.

patriotic-education.rationale: Pupil loyalty rituals are not covered in the sources, and adherents' views vary by country.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Racial preference policy in admissions is not addressed by the movement.

public-money-creation.rationale: Money creation reform is not discussed in the sources.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Theories of capitalist crisis are not part of Islamic feminist analysis.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Not addressed, and anti-colonial sentiment suggests disfavour; inferred.

delink-world-market.rationale: Dependency-theory strategies are not addressed in the movement's sources.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: This Marxist-Leninist claim is not engaged by the movement.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Musawah demands non-discrimination as a basis of all human relations, so a right to discriminate is rejected.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Musawah invokes fundamental rights and constitutional guarantees as a path to equality.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Colonial treaty validity is not addressed, though adherents criticize colonial influence on family law.

elective-rulers.rationale: Equal political participation and citizenship imply elected rulers; inferred.

minority-veto.rationale: The movement rejects vetoes that let a conservative minority block equality reforms.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Not addressed directly; adherents challenge unjust authorities by legal means.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Not addressed; Musawah relies on constitutions and legislatures but also on judicial protection.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Animal ethics does not appear in the sources, so no stance is documented.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Animal use for food or research is not discussed by Islamic feminists.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Aristocratic duty is not part of the movement's thought; its ethic is equality, not obligation of rank.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The movement is activist; Musawah says it is the right and duty of all to contribute to laws and policies.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Critical theory of mass culture is not part of Islamic feminist argument.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Gramscian hegemony theory is not a stated part of the movement's sources.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: World-systems theory is not part of Islamic feminist argument.

native-born-offices.rationale: Equal citizenship and political participation for all contradict reserved offices.

party-own-road.rationale: Communist party independence is irrelevant to this movement.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Development strategy and aid are not discussed in the sources.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Irredentist demands are not addressed by the movement.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Indigenous leadership claims are not part of the movement's agenda.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Constitutional anti-fascism is not discussed in the sources.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Comparisons of fascism and communism are not addressed by the movement.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Musawah compares family-law reform to ending slavery, but the American Civil War question is not addressed.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Monument policy is not covered by the movement's sources.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: The movement centres women's disadvantage and tends to see symmetry arguments as deflection, but it speaks of rights and justice for women and for men.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: SIS campaigns against domestic violence directed at wives and challenged laws protecting abusive husbands; equal-severity framing is not part of its work.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Adherents split between claiming Islamic roots for equality and seeing universal human-rights standards as binding everywhere.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Constitutional accountability and civil participation are central, and the movement opposes unaccountable authority.

paid-care-work.rationale: Musawah notes classical law treated wives as not obliged to do housework and calls for recognition of contributions within the family; inferred.

filial-duty.rationale: Islamic ethics of respect for parents is widely held and not contested by the movement; inferred.

office-by-exam.rationale: Civil service recruitment is not discussed in the sources.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Musawah demands equal right to dissolve marriage and equal rights upon dissolution; Indian petitioners attacked triple talaq.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Imperative mandate for delegates is not addressed by the sources.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Pension design is not discussed by Islamic feminist writers.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Land tenure doctrine is not addressed, apart from equal women's property rights in Musawah.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Legislative budget control is not discussed by the sources.

single-official-language.rationale: Official language policy is not part of the movement.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Foreign land ownership is not covered by the movement's sources.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Musawah calls for substantive equality, but a rule on unequal racial outcomes is not addressed.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Not addressed, though Islamic ethics often criticizes excess.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Not addressed; the movement opposes violent extremist groups; inferred.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Not addressed; the framework of sovereignty and equal citizenship disfavours it; inferred.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Not addressed; Musawah calls for equal economic resources and property, which presupposes existing economic institutions.

abortion-legal.rationale: Adherents are split; Islamic jurisprudence permits abortion in some circumstances and feminist scholars differ, and the movement's texts here do not set a position.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Equality and substantive non-discrimination are core, so correcting injustice is likely welcomed, but the racial case is inferred.

cut-welfare.rationale: Musawah's concern for financial security and dignity suggests opposition to cutting support, though welfare is not addressed.

decide-locally.rationale: Adherents are split: many work at national level to change state family law, others locally.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Musawah leans on CEDAW and international human-rights standards as more in line with Shari'ah than many national laws, which implies a role for international norms.

empower-police-military.rationale: Not addressed; accountability is stressed and security forces have often enforced moral policing, which SIS opposes; inferred.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Musawah states that all human beings are born equal in worth and dignity and that men and women are equal in creation and the afterlife.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Energy policy lies outside the movement's agenda, so no shared position can be drawn.

experts-over-public.rationale: The movement attacks male scholars' monopoly on interpretation, and Anwar says all have an equal right to define Islam.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Foreign investment screening is not a theme of the movement.

free-trade.rationale: Trade policy is not addressed by Musawah or Barlas, so adherents have no shared position.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Islamic feminists argue gender hierarchies come from patriarchal interpretation and social conditions (Barlas, Musawah), though many accept some natural difference and religious framing.

gradual-change.rationale: The movement says laws can evolve with time and place and cites reform through ijtihad, but it also urges that change come now; it is divided in tempo.

land-value-tax.rationale: Land taxation is not part of the movement's agenda, so adherents are indifferent as a group.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Not addressed; Islamic ethics generally disfavors intoxicants so adherents are unlikely to push legalization; inferred.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Not addressed; most adherents work within Islamic moral frameworks and often see sex work as exploitation; inferred.

limit-growth.rationale: Degrowth is not discussed by Islamic feminist writers; no shared position exists.

limit-guns.rationale: Gun control does not feature in the movement's sources and adherents differ by country.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Not addressed; adherents hold varied economic views.

more-religion-public.rationale: Adherents want Islam engaged in public debate but contest which authorities speak for it; some want less religious authority over law, which makes an overall stance split.

nation-first.rationale: The movement works through global networks and human-rights standards, so national-interest-first is disfavored; inferred.

open-borders.rationale: Migration policy is not a stated concern, and adherents are split between universalist and national views.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The core diagnosis of Musawah, Barlas and Mernissi is that law, interpretation and institutions have systematically favored men.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Adherents criticize patriarchal customs but value Muslim heritage; split.

property-fundamental.rationale: Musawah demands equal property rights for women but takes no stance on strength of property rights generally.

public-ownership.rationale: The movement says nothing on ownership of utilities or rail, and adherents range across economic views.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wage levels are not a topic in the Musawah or Barlas literature; adherents take varied economic positions.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Not addressed; a defense of Muslim minorities and universal equality suggest opposition; inferred.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Corporate regulation is not discussed in the sources; the movement's concerns are family law and religious interpretation.

rehabilitation.rationale: Not addressed beyond opposing hudud punishments; adherents are not committed either way.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Adherents are split between free expression and protection from hate speech against Muslims.

revolution-justified.rationale: The movement pursues reform and campaigns against extremist groups; inferred.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Adherents are split, with some progressive Muslims supportive and many unwilling to take a position; the movement's core texts are silent.

socialized-markets.rationale: Market socialism is not addressed in the sources; adherents' economic views vary.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Industrial policy is not discussed, and Musawah's texts concern law and family, not investment.

state-harmful.rationale: The movement depends on the state and constitution to guarantee equality and to reform family law.

strong-leader.rationale: Musawah promotes equal participation and constitutional guarantees; unchecked leaders are disfavored.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Not addressed; opposition to moral policing and state abuse suggests wariness; inferred.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Protectionism does not appear in Islamic feminist sources; adherents are indifferent as a movement.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Not addressed; Musawah's inheritance demand concerns equal shares between sexes, not taxation.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Tax rates on high earners are outside the movement's gender-and-family-law agenda.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The movement makes no claims about technology as a solution to social problems.

traditional-family.rationale: Musawah wants marriage as a partnership of equals, replacing the classical model of husband domination and wife obedience, though adherents value family strongly.

unions-good.rationale: Not addressed, though labour rights are listed among areas affected by gender inequality.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Musawah wants equal property rights for women, but nothing in it favors small ownership over concentration.

worker-ownership.rationale: Worker-owned firms are not a theme in Islamic feminist texts, and adherents hold no common view.

corporate-influence.rationale: Not a central issue for the movement; its focus is on gender, family law and religious authority.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Groups such as Sisters in Islam rely on foreign and international funding and have been targeted by state restrictions; inferred opposition.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Inferred from emphasis on women's autonomy and choice in marriage and parenting, which sits poorly with state pressure to bear more children.

job-guarantee.rationale: The Musawah Framework calls for women's economic rights and equal property, but not a state job guarantee.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The movement works for reform within constitutions and the law, relying on legal equality and CEDAW, so it affirms a duty to obey legitimate law; inferred.

non-intervention.rationale: Islamic feminists use international human-rights standards yet resist Western intervention framed as rescuing Muslim women; adherents split.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The movement rests on justice and equality for all, and opposes discrimination and scapegoating of groups; inferred from its human-rights framing.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: The movement seeks to reform legal marriage so that it gives women equal rights in divorce, property and parenting, not to abolish it.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Inferred from the calls for transparent, accountable law-making and women's equal voice in defining law and religion.

informal-organisation.rationale: Musawah and Sisters in Islam are formal NGOs and coalitions that lobby for legal reform; the movement does not favour purely informal groups.

national-law-over-international.rationale: The Musawah Framework invokes CEDAW and international human-rights standards alongside constitutions, so the movement does not place national law above them.

religious-nation.rationale: Islamic feminists work within an Islamic framework and many accept Islam in national identity, but they press for equal citizenship for all; adherents split.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Inferred from the movement's human-rights and equality framing; not addressed.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Not addressed; the movement is silent on public service delivery.

religion-illusion.rationale: Islamic feminism is faith-based and argues the Qur'an itself supports equality; religion is treated as enduring, not an illusion.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: The movement works through reinterpretation and legal reform of family law within the existing order rather than economic transformation; inferred.

socialized-care.rationale: Not addressed; family care is treated within reformed marriage law, not public services.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the movement's open, reformist stance toward language and tradition.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Not addressed; the movement works within existing states and families, so communal reorganization is inferred to be rejected.

majority-settlement.rationale: Not addressed; state-steered settlement conflicts with the movement's equality and rights framing.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Not an issue the movement addresses; adherents are split on territorial claims, so it is inferred as neutral.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Its human-rights and justice framework rejects genocide denial; the movement does not address it directly, so this is inferred from its principles.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: The movement centres on women and family law and rarely addresses this; its rights-based, ijtihad-driven reading of equality points against criminalisation, but adherents are cautious and the answer is inferred.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The Framework for Action calls for constitutional guarantees, public participation and rights standards, which implies free opposition; inferred, not directly addressed.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: It argues Islam's core is justice and opposes coercion by patriarchal authorities, which points against state punishment of belief; it does not address blasphemy law directly, so this is inferred.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Anti-colonial and justice-centred, but not discussed; inferred from its equality and rights principles.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Not addressed by the movement; adherents' views on armed resistance are not documented, so it is inferred as split.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: It seeks reform through reinterpretation, constitutions and legal change, and critiques patriarchal rulers' claims to religious authority; it rejects violent overthrow, though this is inferred from its method.

participatory-democracy.rationale: It demands women's equal voice in decisions about family and religion, which implies broad participation; not stated in the sources as a general principle, so inferred.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: The Musawah Framework holds that gender discrimination interacts with other injustices of class, race and politics and must be addressed together; the framework text speaks of overlapping inequalities.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: The movement does not address transgender recognition and adherents are split; inferred as neutral.

assisted-dying.rationale: Not addressed; adherents are split between religious objections to ending life and bodily-autonomy arguments.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: It combines faith with equality, rather than discarding either side; it does not frame itself this way, and the answer is inferred.

alienated-labor.rationale: Not addressed; the movement has no stated view on alienation in wage labour.

islam-incompatible.rationale: It holds that Islam itself is egalitarian and compatible with human rights and modern constitutions, and blames patriarchal readings rather than Islam; stated across its founding texts.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Adherents hold that God is the ultimate source of justice but argue through constitutions, citizenship and equal rights for all; Musawah calls for state law grounded in equality rather than rule by religious authorities, so it is split towards popular authority.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: It defends women's agency and choice in dress against both coerced veiling and bans; it does not discuss state institutions directly, so this is inferred.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Its commitment to women's access to justice implies support, but nondisclosure agreements are not addressed; inferred.

social-market-economy.rationale: Not addressed; adherents hold a range of economic views.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Not addressed; no stated view on armed forces among adherents.

rich-first.rationale: Its emphasis on equal rights and justice for all suggests opposition to uneven development, but this is inferred.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Not addressed; adherents hold no common view on alliances.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Inferred from the movement's demand for equal citizenship and accountable, rule-governed reform; hereditary succession is not discussed.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Inferred: the movement is about gender and family law and takes no collective position on bank ownership.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Not addressed; adherents are likely split and the movement's focus is family law, not international finance.

property-franchise.rationale: Musawah's Framework rests on equality and non-discrimination, which a wealth or tax test for voting contradicts.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Inferred from the argument that patriarchal readings of scripture, not Islam, justify subordination, and from Islamic stewardship ethics; ecofeminism is not a core claim.

reification.rationale: Not addressed; a Marxist concept the movement does not use, so no stance is inferred.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Not addressed; adherents focus on religious and family authority rather than media ownership.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Inferred from Musawah's push for codified, equal family laws applied by courts rather than discretionary rulings.

racial-franchise.rationale: The Framework grounds reform in equality and justice for all, so limiting political rights to one racial or ethnic group is rejected.

online-participation.rationale: Inferred: the movement seeks women's equal voice in public life, and its groups organise online, but it takes no stated position.

open-government-data.rationale: Inferred from the Framework's emphasis on accountability and constitutional and human-rights standards.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Musawah demands equal rights in choosing a spouse, which cuts against bans on marrying across faiths, though adherents work within Islamic texts.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Targeting a religious minority commercially contradicts the Framework's justice and non-discrimination principles.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Inferred: the movement demands women's equal voice in public and religious decision-making, which suits broad citizen deliberation, but no source discusses sortition.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Its core demand is ijtihad: reading the Qur'an anew and challenging patriarchal classical jurisprudence in light of justice and present conditions.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The movement stresses justice and dignity in access to resources, which loosely implies concern about wealth domination; inferred, not a focus.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: The movement focuses on family law and religious authority; Muslim feminists are divided on LGBT questions and it has no clear position on military service.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Islamic feminism works within an Islamic framework and seeks equality through faith, so state promotion of unbelief is contrary to its premise.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: The movement seeks reform of law and equal justice under constitutions and rights standards rather than abolition of state institutions; inferred.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The movement does not address consociational power-sharing; its legal framework is equal citizenship, but communal representation for religious groups is a separate matter.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Zakat and communal giving are part of Islamic practice, but the movement also demands state legal guarantees; adherents are not clearly aligned.

term-limits.rationale: Not discussed by the movement; its concerns are family law and religious interpretation.

vote-delegation.rationale: The movement works through constitutions, courts and legislatures for legal reform, which implies conventional representation rather than delegable voting; inferred.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: The movement does not address extinction risk and its principles give no clear direction.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Advocates support women as clergy, mosque administrators, judges and interpreters, and hold that women have an equal right to define Islam.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Musawah's Framework calls for equality in marriage and challenges the doctrine of male guardianship (qiwama) as authority over wives.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: The Musawah Framework concerns equal citizenship for women and does not address the voting rights of foreign residents.

rent-control.rationale: Islamic feminism concerns gender, family law and religious authority; housing is not addressed.

abolish-ip.rationale: Intellectual property is not addressed by the movement.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Inferred from the Framework's rights-based approach, which values voluntary association and women's freedom.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Nuclear weapons are not addressed by the movement.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Foreign military bases are not addressed by the movement.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Inferred from the Framework's reliance on human-rights standards such as CEDAW, which favour official acknowledgement of abuses.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Islamic feminism is not mainly about economic structure, and Islamic law's restrictions on interest and its support for earnings by women both feature.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Islamic ethics as the movement reads them permit defence of life, but the sources do not address this directly.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Nation and ummah are not addressed by the movement, and its thinkers are split on nationalism.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: The Qur'anic reading of Wadud and Barlas holds that patriarchy comes from interpretation, not that sexes are made by culture; this is inferred.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: The Framework speaks for women with differing situations, and the sources do not say whether the category is fixed.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Honouring martyrs is not addressed by the movement.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The movement pursues reform through reinterpretation, constitutions and human-rights law, not a cosmic struggle; this is inferred.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Diaspora and homeland are not addressed by the movement.

culture-before-state.rationale: Cultural renewal versus state-building is not addressed by the movement.

god-not-male.rationale: Barlas and Wadud argue that the Qur'an does not present God as male and that patriarchal readings gave God a male image.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Islamic feminists keep the Qur'an authoritative but hold that patriarchal interpretations and jurisprudence must be set aside where they deny women's equality.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Inferred from the Framework's call for equality and citizenship regardless of group.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Regional borders for peoples are not addressed by the movement.

independent-unions.rationale: Inferred from the movement's rights and justice commitments; unions are not discussed in the sources.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: The movement is about gender, family law and religious authority and takes no stand on socialism.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Inferred from commitment to dignity and equal access to resources; not a stated issue.

family-wage.rationale: Musawah challenges male financial guardianship in marriage and calls for equal rights and responsibilities, which cuts against the male-breadwinner premise.

person-over-state.rationale: Inferred from the Framework's reliance on constitutions and human-rights standards that protect the person against abusive authority.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The movement is faith-based and argues the Qur'an itself supports equality, so adherents take a religious view of the person.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Inferred from the movement's insistence on equality beyond group lines and its use of universal human-rights standards.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Not an issue the movement addresses; Islamic feminists work within national legal systems and adherents hold no shared view on language-based nationhood.

communal-electorates.rationale: The movement seeks equal citizenship and equal family law within states, so separate religious electorates sit poorly with its reliance on constitutions and common rights; inferred, not stated.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: The movement does not address foreign-plot claims; adherents differ and often face both state and Western pressures.

free-public-college.rationale: Not a stated concern; inferred from the Islamic and rights-based emphasis on justice and education as an equal entitlement.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Environmental taxation lies outside the movement's concerns and no shared adherent view is documented.

future-generations.rationale: Not discussed directly; stewardship (khalifa) in the Qur'anic reading the movement defends implies a duty to later generations, inferred at low confidence.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Adherents split: the movement stresses equality and rejects fixed gender essences in the Qur'anic reading, yet also values women's voice in defining Islam and public life.

arms-reduction.rationale: Not addressed by the movement and no shared view among adherents.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Not addressed by the movement; adherents hold no common position on diplomatic secrecy.

capital-controls.rationale: Economic controls are outside the movement's concerns and adherents hold no shared view.

missingStatements.text: Muslim family law should give women and men equal rights in marriage, divorce, custody and inheritance.
missingStatements.rationale: Musawah's Framework calls for equal rights in choosing a spouse, dissolving marriage, property, inheritance and parenting.

missingStatements.text: Polygamy should be prohibited or made strictly conditional by law.
missingStatements.rationale: Sisters in Islam argues polygamy is conditional and promotes monogamy as the Qur'anic ideal, and petitioners in India challenged polygyny.
missingStatements.declined: Narrow policy detail; equal-moral-worth covers equal family-law rights.

missingStatements.text: Women should be able to serve as religious leaders, judges and interpreters of religious texts.
missingStatements.rationale: Advocates support women as clergy, mosque administrators and judges, and Anwar says women have an equal right to define Islam.

missingStatements.text: Religious authorities should not have the power to punish those who leave their religion.
missingStatements.rationale: Sisters in Islam opposed Kelantan's criminal code and apostasy bill punishing those who left the faith.

notes: Secular Muslim feminists such as Mahnaz Afkhami reject the label and would answer secularism and scripture statements differently. Adherents differ on veiling bans, personal law versus civil law in minority settings, and the weight of hadith.
